newsitem.title: UK: Internet soap opera offers to put ads in storyline.
newsitem.headline: Internet soap opera offers to put ads in storyline.

text.p: Feeney Tralee is a hugely ambitious, philandering Irishman with a background in advertising and devilish good looks. He is also fictitious.
Tralee is one of the leading characters in a soap opera running on the Internet that is offering advertisers the chance to feature in its story lines.
Called the Bath Soap, the weekly series is set in a fictional shopping centre and features the kind of adjective-laden writing style typical of romance novels.

"The story delves into the lives, passions and motivations of a group of characters and their endless plotting and scheming," Enriqueta Koch de Gooreynd of Bath-based APC, which is producing the serial, told Reuters on Friday.
Advertisers will be able to insert their name or brand into the story line for 25 pounds ($40) per episode. For 70 pounds they can buy a full page ad.

"People are tired of having ads rammed down their throats. With the Bath Soap approach nobody feels pressurised. If the story line excites their interest in a particular product then the user can take a further look at what is on offer", she said.
APC is currently talking to a number of undisclosed companies about advertising in the serial.
Advertising on the Internet remains in its infancy, with Web Site publishers and advertisers struggling to find ways to get the attention of Web surfers.
Soap operas on the Internet's World Wide Web pages are becoming increasingly popular. It is estimated there up to a 100 serials updated monthly, weekly or even daily on the Internet.
The subject matter is diverse and ranges from corporate intrigue to science fiction fantasies, but all follow the traditional TV soap format and feature a cliff-hanger at the end of each episode.

APC will not reveal how much "Bath Soap" cost to set up. But in the United States a drama called "Madeline's Mind," created by Digital Planet, cost $250,000. Another called "The East Village" took $600,000 to develop and requires $15,000 per week to maintain.
